feedback: If a learner is unsure how to tag the grasshopper, name it incomplete metamorphosis: it is still metamorphosis because the nymph develops gradually (including wing buds growing into wings over successive moults), but it has no pupa stage and none of the butterfly's dramatic rebuilding of the body inside the pupa. Contrast complete metamorphosis (butterfly, through a pupa) with incomplete metamorphosis (grasshopper) and with true direct development in birds and mammals, where no larval or nymph stage occurs.

If a learner calls the kitten-to-cat or chick-to-bird change 'metamorphosis', ask them to point to what changed shape versus what just got bigger; reinforce that growth in size with the same body form is direct development, not metamorphosis.
If stages are ordered wrongly, prompt them to find the egg/birth start and trace one step at a time to the adult that reproduces.

When a tag is correctly justified by observed change-of-form, name the principle back: a change of body form across the cycle is metamorphosis (dramatic and via a pupa = complete; gradual via nymphs = incomplete); the same body form just getting bigger is direct development.
activities.intendedInsight: Metamorphosis is a change of body FORM within one individual's life cycle (not merely getting bigger). In complete metamorphosis (butterfly) the change is dramatic and passes through a pupa; in incomplete metamorphosis (grasshopper) the change is gradual through nymph stages that already resemble the adult, with no pupa — but both are metamorphosis. Amphibians also metamorphose. Birds and mammals show direct development: the young already resembles the adult and simply grows larger with no larval or nymph stage.
learnerActions: Arrange the stages of each cycle in correct order into a ring: mammal (born live → grows → adult, no change of form); bird (egg → chick → adult); amphibian (egg → tadpole → frog); insect complete (egg → larva/caterpillar → pupa → adult butterfly); insect incomplete (egg → nymph → adult grasshopper).

Run two cycles at once and watch each transition: the tadpole sprouting legs and losing its tail to become a frog; the caterpillar shedding its skin to form a pupa (chrysalis) and later emerging as a butterfly; the grasshopper nymph moulting through stages that already resemble the adult while gradually developing (wing buds growing into wings), with no pupa; the chick and the puppy simply getting bigger with the same basic body form.
Compare the butterfly cycle directly beside the grasshopper cycle and describe in your own words how a complete transformation through a pupa differs from gradual change through nymph stages.

Tag each completed cycle — metamorphosis (complete, like the butterfly through a pupa; or incomplete, like the grasshopper through nymph stages; the amphibian also metamorphoses) versus direct development (bird, mammal) — and justify the tag by pointing to what you observed changing (or not changing) in body form and whether a pupa stage is present.
activities.title: Build and run four life cycles side by side

feedback: If a learner cannot say where two cycles differ, ask them to find the one stage where body form changes (pupa for the butterfly; tadpole→frog for the amphibian) and compare it with a bird or mammal whose young keeps the same form.
Prompt learners to use correct terms (egg, larva, pupa, nymph, adult) as they describe each stage.
Reinforce that even very different-looking cycles still contain birth/hatching, growth, reproduction and death.
activities.intendedInsight: The canonical cycle diagram makes the stages and their order explicit and names the vocabulary, while a compare view localises where metamorphosis differs from direct development; all cycles share the same universal stages.
learnerActions: Study labelled circular life-cycle diagrams for a mammal, bird, amphibian and insect; for each stage, uncover or note what happens at that point in the cycle.
Overlay or place two cycles next to each other and highlight exactly where one cycle changes body form and the other does not.
Trace the shared ring of universal stages — birth/hatching, growth, reproduction, death — underneath every cycle to see diversity within a common frame.
activities.title: Explore labelled cycle diagrams and compare

feedback: If a learner sorts all insects as complete metamorphosis, show the grasshopper incomplete pathway (no pupa, nymph resembles adult and develops gradually) — still metamorphosis, but incomplete. Dragonflies also have no pupa, but their underwater nymphs look quite different from the adult.
If a learner classifies the chick as metamorphosis, point out that it already resembles the adult and only grows larger with no larval or nymph stage — direct development.
For a wrong sequence, have them locate the pupa (if any) and check it sits between larva and adult; for an incomplete cycle, check that nymph stages sit between egg and adult with no pupa.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can both order the stages and classify each group by the change-of-form criterion, distinguishing complete from incomplete metamorphosis while keeping both on the metamorphosis side, and separating these from the direct development of birds and mammals.
learnerActions: Put the stages of each cycle in order, including the butterfly (egg → larva → pupa → adult).

Sort the example animals into 'undergoes metamorphosis' (amphibians such as the frog; insects such as the butterfly and grasshopper) versus 'direct development' (birds, mammals), and explain the sorting rule.

Match each group to its cycle type and distinguish complete metamorphosis (egg→larva→pupa→adult) from incomplete (egg→nymph→adult), using the presence or absence of a pupa as the tell — remembering that incomplete metamorphosis is still metamorphosis.
Answer: a chick hatches looking like a small fluffy version of the adult — is that metamorphosis or direct development, and why?
activities.title: Classify and sequence cycles

feedback: If a learner says the caterpillar dies and a different animal emerges, trace the continuity of the one individual: the same body is extensively rebuilt inside the chrysalis, not replaced by a new creature.
If a learner calls kitten-to-cat metamorphosis, contrast complete change of form (caterpillar→butterfly) with same-form growth (kitten→cat); only a change of body form counts as metamorphosis.
If a learner classifies a tadpole as a baby fish, follow it through growing legs and lungs and losing its tail into a frog — one animal metamorphosing.
activities.intendedInsight: Inside the pupa (chrysalis), a single individual's caterpillar body is reorganised into the adult butterfly — it is the same animal, not a replacement — which is a complete change of form; a kitten growing into a cat keeps the same body form and just gets bigger (direct development). A tadpole is a young frog, not a fish.
learnerActions: Discuss: 'A caterpillar turns into a butterfly. Is that butterfly the SAME creature the caterpillar was, or a different animal?' and give your reasons.
Discuss: 'Does a kitten change in that same big way as it grows into a cat — why or why not?'

Respond to probes: What happens inside the chrysalis — does the caterpillar keep its caterpillar body? Is a tadpole a baby fish or a baby frog, and how can you tell? Name an animal group that does NOT go through metamorphosis and say how its young grow instead.
Explain how you can tell whether an insect transforms completely (through a pupa) or changes gradually (through nymph stages), using the butterfly and grasshopper as examples.
activities.title: Talk it through: same creature or different animal?
